lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: MIG welding, also called Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), is the workhorse of modern metal fabrication. In Africa, where industries from auto repair to construction are booming, MIG welding offers speed, versatility, and ease of learning. Unlike stick welding, MIG uses a continuously fed wire electrode and a shielding gas to protect the weld pool. This means you can weld thin sheet metal or thick plates with the same machine by adjusting voltage and wire speed. For a small workshop in Nairobi or Lagos, a 200-amp MIG welder running on 220V single phase can handle most jobs. The key advantage is productivity: you don't stop to change electrodes every few inches. You can weld steel, stainless, and aluminum (with the right setup). In Africa, MIG is increasingly used in fabrication of gates, window frames, truck bodies, and agricultural equipment. It also produces less slag than stick welding, so cleanup is faster. However, MIG requires a shielding gas cylinder, typically 75% Argon/25% CO2 for steel. This adds cost, but the speed and quality pay off. Learning MIG opens doors to jobs in manufacturing, repair shops, and even overseas contracts. This module will take you from setting up the machine to running clean beads on different joints. You'll learn to troubleshoot common defects and work safely. By the end, you'll be able to produce strong, neat welds that meet professional standards. Remember, MIG is a skill best learned by doing. So get your gloves on and let's start.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To MIG weld effectively, you need the right tools and materials. First, a MIG welder: for most African workshops, a 200-amp machine like the Lincoln Electric Power MIG 210 MP or a Chinese equivalent (e.g., Andeli MIG-200) works well. Ensure it can run on 220V single-phase power, common in many African countries. You'll need a shielding gas cylinder: for mild steel, use 75% Argon/25% CO2 (often called C25). In South Africa, Afrox supplies this; in Kenya, BOC. A flowmeter regulator is essential to set gas flow to 10-15 CFH (cubic feet per hour). Without gas, your weld will be porous. Next, filler wire: for mild steel, use ER70S-6 wire in 0.8mm or 1.0mm diameter. For stainless, ER308L; for aluminum, ER4043. Buy quality wire from welding suppliers, not cheap uncoated wire that rusts. You'll need a wire brush, angle grinder with grinding and cutting discs, and clamps to hold your work. Personal protective equipment: auto-darkening welding helmet (shade 10-13), leather gloves, flame-resistant jacket, and steel-toe boots. For practice, get mild steel plates: 3mm to 6mm thick, cut into 100mm x 150mm pieces. Clean them with a grinder to remove mill scale and rust. A wire cutter and nozzle gel (anti-spatter) help keep the torch clean. Finally, a good workbench and a fire extinguisher. In many African cities, you can find these at industrial areas like Kariobangi in Nairobi or Alaba in Lagos. Don't skimp on gas or wire; poor consumables lead to poor welds.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to make a sound MIG weld. First, set up your machine: connect the gas cylinder to the regulator, set flow to 12 CFH. Install the wire spool, feed it through the drive rolls (tension should be snug but not crushing the wire), and into the torch liner. Use the correct contact tip for your wire size (0.8mm tip for 0.8mm wire). Set voltage and wire speed according to the thickness of your metal. For 3mm steel, start with voltage 18-19V and wire speed 3.5-4.0 m/min (check your machine's chart). Second, prepare your metal: grind the edges to bare metal, clamp it securely. For a butt joint, leave a 1-2mm gap. Third, position yourself: hold the torch at a 10-15 degree push angle (tilted away from the direction of travel). This gives better gas coverage and penetration. Fourth, strike the arc: touch the wire to the metal, pull the trigger, and move. Maintain a consistent travel speedâabout 3-5 mm per second for 3mm steel. Keep the contact tip to work distance (CTWD) at 10-12mm. Too close, and you'll clog the tip; too far, and you lose gas coverage. Fifth, watch the weld pool: it should be a smooth, oval shape. If it's too fluid, reduce voltage; if it's too cold and lumpy, increase voltage or wire speed. For a fillet weld, angle the torch at 45 degrees into the joint. Practice on scrap until you can run a straight bead without stopping. Remember to clean the nozzle regularly with pliers to remove spatter. After welding, let it cool, then chip off any slag (though MIG produces little) and inspect. A good weld is uniform, with fine ripples and no undercut or porosity.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Even experienced welders make mistakes. Here are common MIG problems and how to fix them. First, porosity (holes in the weld): usually caused by insufficient gas flow, windy conditions, or dirty metal. Check your gas cylinder isn't empty, set flow to 12-15 CFH, and weld indoors or use a wind screen. Clean metal with a grinder before welding. Second, spatter: excessive spatter means voltage too low or wire speed too high. Increase voltage slightly or reduce wire speed. Also, ensure you're using the correct polarity: for MIG, the torch is positive (DCEP). If you accidentally set DCEN, you'll get poor penetration and spatter. Third, burn-through: on thin metal, you may blow holes. Reduce voltage and wire speed, or use a thicker wire (0.9mm) and move faster. For 1.5mm sheet, try 16V and 2.5 m/min. Fourth, lack of penetration: the weld sits on top without fusing. Increase voltage and wire speed, or slow down your travel. Also, ensure your joint has a small gap. Fifth, wire stubbing: the wire pushes back into the torch. This happens when wire speed is too high or voltage too low. Adjust the settings. Sixth, birdnesting: wire tangles at the drive rolls. This is caused by too much tension on the spool or a kinked liner. Check the spool tension and replace the liner if worn. Seventh, undercut: a groove melted into the base metal along the weld toe. This weakens the joint. Reduce travel speed or increase wire speed to fill the groove. In Africa, power fluctuations can affect weld quality. Use a voltage stabilizer if your machine is sensitive. Always practice on scrap before welding a critical part. Keep a notebook of settings that work for different thicknesses.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: MIG welding is safe if you follow basic rules. First, protect your eyes and skin: the arc emits intense UV and IR radiation. Always wear an auto-darkening helmet with shade 10-13. Never look at the arc with naked eyes. Wear leather gloves, a flame-resistant jacket (leather or cotton), and closed shoes. Synthetic clothing can melt and stick to skin. Second, prevent fires: welding sparks can travel up to 10 meters. Clear the area of flammable materials like paper, cloth, petrol, and paint thinners. Keep a fire extinguisher (dry powder or CO2) within reach. In many African workshops, wooden structures are common; use a welding blanket to protect them. Third, ensure proper ventilation: MIG welding produces fumes, especially when welding galvanized or painted metal. Work in a well-ventilated area or use a fume extractor. If you feel dizzy, stop and get fresh air. Fourth, handle gas cylinders safely: secure them upright with a chain or strap. Keep them away from heat and never roll them on their side. When not in use, close the valve and remove the regulator. Fifth, avoid electric shock: check cables for damage, ensure the machine is grounded, and never weld in wet conditions. Wear dry gloves. Sixth, maintain your equipment: inspect the torch liner, contact tip, and nozzle daily. Replace worn parts. Clean the drive rolls. A well-maintained machine gives better welds and is safer. Seventh, practice good posture: weld at a comfortable height to avoid back strain. Use a stool or adjustable table. Finally, never weld alone if possible; have someone nearby in case of emergency. In Africa, where access to medical help may be limited, prevention is critical. Follow these practices and you'll weld for years without injury.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: This exercise will build your MIG skills step by step. You'll need: a MIG welder, 75/25 Ar/CO2 gas, ER70S-6 0.8mm wire, mild steel plates (6 pieces of 3mm x 50mm x 100mm), angle grinder, clamps, and PPE. First, set your machine: voltage 18V, wire speed 3.5 m/min, gas flow 12 CFH. Practice on a scrap plate: run 5 straight beads, each about 75mm long, overlapping slightly. Focus on keeping a consistent travel speed and CTWD. After each bead, inspect for uniformity. Adjust settings if needed. Second, tack weld two plates together in a butt joint with a 1mm gap. Make tacks at both ends and the middle. Then run a continuous bead along the joint. Aim for full penetration; you should see a slight weld bead on the back side. If not, increase voltage to 19V and slow down. Third, do a T-joint: place one plate vertically on another horizontally. Tack weld, then run a fillet weld on both sides. Angle the torch at 45 degrees. Use a slight push angle. Fourth, try a lap joint: overlap two plates by 25mm, clamp, and weld along the edge. Fifth, inspect your welds: look for porosity, undercut, and spatter. Use a wire brush to clean. If you find defects, cut out the weld with a grinder and redo. Repeat until you can produce clean, strong welds. Finally, test your weld strength: clamp one plate in a vise and hit the other with a hammer. The weld should not break; the metal should bend. If it breaks, your penetration was insufficient. Record your settings for each joint type. In Africa, where materials may vary, always test on scrap first. This exercise takes about 2 hours. Practice daily for a week and you'll see rapid improvement.

quiz.q: What does MIG stand for?
quiz.explanation: MIG stands for Metal Inert Gas, though it is now often called Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW).

quiz.q: Which shielding gas is commonly used for MIG welding mild steel?
quiz.explanation: A mix of 75% Argon and 25% CO2 provides good arc stability and penetration for mild steel.

quiz.q: What is the typical wire diameter for welding 3mm mild steel with a 200-amp MIG welder?
quiz.explanation: 0.8mm wire is versatile and works well for thin to medium steel with a 200-amp machine.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gas flow rate for MIG welding in a draft-free environment?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 CFH provides adequate shielding without wasting gas or causing turbulence.

quiz.q: Which polarity is used for MIG welding?
quiz.explanation: MIG welding uses DCEP, meaning the torch is positive, which gives better penetration and stable arc.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the contact tip in a MIG torch?
options: A) To guide the wire and transfer current
quiz.explanation: The contact tip guides the wire and conducts welding current to it.

quiz.q: What causes porosity in a MIG weld?
options: B) Insufficient gas flow or dirty metal
quiz.explanation: Porosity is typically caused by lack of shielding gas coverage or contaminants on the metal.

quiz.q: What is the correct contact tip to work distance (CTWD) for MIG welding?
quiz.explanation: A CTWD of 10-12mm ensures good gas coverage and stable arc without overheating the torch.

quiz.q: Which type of wire is used for welding stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: ER308L is the common filler wire for welding 304 stainless steel.

quiz.q: What is 'birdnesting' in MIG welding?
options: A) A type of weld defect
B) Wire tangling at the drive rolls
C) A method to clean the nozzle
quiz.explanation: Birdnesting occurs when the wire feed gets tangled, often due to incorrect drive roll tension.

quiz.q: What should you do if you experience burn-through on thin metal?
options: C) Reduce voltage and wire speed
quiz.explanation: Reducing heat input by lowering voltage and wire speed prevents burn-through on thin materials.

quiz.q: Which PPE is essential for MIG welding?
quiz.explanation: An auto-darkening helmet protects eyes from intense UV and IR radiation.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important in MIG welding?
options: A) To keep the welder cool
B) To remove fumes and gases
quiz.explanation: Welding fumes can be harmful; proper ventilation removes them from the breathing zone.

quiz.q: What is the recommended push angle for MIG welding?
quiz.explanation: A slight push angle (10-15 degrees) improves visibility and gas coverage.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of excessive spatter?
options: B) Too low voltage or too high wire speed
quiz.explanation: Low voltage or high wire speed can cause the wire to stub and create spatter.

quiz.q: How can you test the strength of a practice weld?
options: B) Bend test with a hammer
quiz.explanation: A bend test can reveal lack of penetration or weak welds.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding galvanized steel?
options: B) Grind off the galvanized coating
quiz.explanation: Galvanized coating produces toxic fumes; grinding it off reduces hazard.

quiz.q: Which component regulates the gas flow from the cylinder?
quiz.explanation: The regulator reduces cylinder pressure and a flowmeter sets the flow rate.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade for a MIG welding helmet?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10-13 is suitable for most MIG welding currents.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of anti-spatter nozzle gel?
options: B) To prevent spatter from sticking to the nozzle
quiz.explanation: Nozzle gel makes it easier to remove spatter from the nozzle.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of insufficient gas flow?
quiz.explanation: Inadequate gas coverage leads to porosity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good practice when welding in a workshop?
options: B) Keep a fire extinguisher nearby
quiz.explanation: A fire extinguisher is essential for safety in case of sparks igniting materials.

quiz.q: What is the typical voltage range for welding 3mm mild steel with 0.8mm wire?
quiz.explanation: 18-20V is a good starting range for 3mm steel with 0.8mm wire.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a wire liner in a MIG torch?
options: A) To guide the wire from the drive rolls to the contact tip
quiz.explanation: The liner guides the wire smoothly and prevents kinking.

quiz.q: What should you do if the wire feed is erratic?
options: B) Check drive roll tension and liner
quiz.explanation: Erratic feed often results from incorrect drive roll tension or a worn liner.

quiz.q: Which joint requires a push angle for best results?
quiz.explanation: A push angle is generally recommended for all joint types in MIG welding.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of MIG welding over stick welding?
options: B) No need for shielding gas
C) Continuous wire feed for higher productivity
D) Better for outdoor windy conditions
quiz.explanation: MIG allows continuous welding without changing electrodes, increasing speed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended travel speed for welding 3mm steel?
quiz.explanation: 3-5 mm/s is a typical travel speed for 3mm steel to ensure proper fusion.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a flowmeter?
options: A) To measure gas flow rate
quiz.explanation: A flowmeter indicates the rate of shielding gas flow in CFH or L/min.

quiz.q: What should you do after finishing a weld to ensure safety?
options: A) Leave the torch on the ground
B) Close the gas valve and turn off the machine
quiz.explanation: Closing the gas valve and turning off the machine prevents accidents and gas leaks.
